title: EIP-8452: Jump and Call Tables for the EVM
description: JUMPV and CALLSUBV, a multi-way jump and call through a table of destinations in the code
author: Greg Colvin (@gcolvin) <greg@colvin.org>
bodyPreview: ## Abstract Two instructions. `JUMPV` jumps to one of a table of destinations, chosen by a case on the *data stack*; `CALLSUBV` calls one. The table is data in the code, and its position is on the stack, so the instructions take no immediate data and behave identically in ordinary and validated code. In ordinary code they are as dynamic and as checked as `JUMP`; in `MAGIC` code the `PUSH` before them makes the dispatch static, and validation proves every destination before the code is deployed. They are the multi-way jump and call for which [EIP-7979](./eip-7979.md) reserved `0xBE` and `0xBD`: a switch, a state machine, or a contract's dispatch on its selector becomes one instruction rather than a chain of comparisons. *Note: Significant assistance from AI is acknowledged, primarily for the reference implementation and its tests.* ## Motivation Validated code has no computed jumps: [EIP-8337](./eip-8337.md) requires the destination of every jump and call to be a constant in the code, which is what makes its control flow static and its validation linear. The price is dispatch. Choosing among *N* destinations by a value takes *N* comparisons and jumps, or a tree of them, where legacy code takes one computed `JUMP` through a table in memory. Every contract pays this at its entry, dispatching on its selector; interpreters and state machines pay it in their inner loops; and compilers, which lower a `switch` to a jump table on every other machine, cannot here. A table in the code gives the dispatch back without giving up the proof. The destinations are constants, so validation checks each of them as it checks any other; a validator or a translator sees every successor of a `JUMPV` and every callee of a `CALLSUBV`, and a `CALLSUBV`'s callees are proven to agree on what they take from the stack and leave on it. The instruction executes in constant time: a bounds comparison and a table read. ## Specification > *The key words MUST and MUST NOT in this Specification are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119 and RFC 8174.* The *data stack*, the *return stack*, the *PC*, a *return address* and a *subroutine* are as [EIP-7979](./eip-7979.md) defines them; `MAGIC` code, `valid` code, an *instruction*, *reachable*, an *entry*, a *stack offset* and a *net stack effect* are as [EIP-8337](./eip-8337.md) defines them. A *table* is a *count* byte followed by *count* + 1 *destinations* of two bytes each, big-endian, each a position in the code, counted from its first byte. A *table* lies anywhere in the code; it is data, and its position is an operand of the instructions below. The *case* is an item popped from the *data stack*; it chooses *destination* number *case* in the *table*, counting from zero, or the last *destination* when *case* exceeds the *count*. Neither instruction takes immediate data, so JUMPDEST analysis is unchanged, and both behave identically in ordinary and `MAGIC` code. ### `JUMPV (0xBE)` Transfers control to one of the *destinations* in a *table*. 1. Pop the position of the *table* from the top of the *data stack*. 2. Pop the *case* from the top of the *data stack*. 3. Set the *PC* to the *destination* the *case* chooses. If the *table* does not lie within the code, or the *destination* is not a `JUMPDEST` or a `CALLDEST`, execution is in an exceptional halting state. Jumping to a `CALLDEST` enters the *subroutine* without pushing a *return address*, as `JUMP` does. The gas cost is *high* (10). ### `CALLSUBV (0xBD)` Transfers control to one of the *subroutines* whose entries are in a *table*. 1. Pop the position of the *table* from the top of the *data stack*. 2. Pop the *case* from the top of the *data stack*. 3. Push the *return address*, *PC* + 1, to the *return stack*. 4. Set the *PC* to the *destination* the *case* chooses. If the *table* does not lie within the code, or the *destination* is not a `CALLDEST`, or the *return stack* already holds 1024 items, execution is in an exceptional halting state. The gas cost is *high* (10). ### Validation The validation rules of the fork that adopts this EIP extend the constraints of [EIP-8337](./eip-8337.md) to the two instructions, as Constraints 2 and 3 cover `JUMP`, `JUMPI` and `CALLSUB`: * Every *reachable* `JUMPV` and `CALLSUBV` MUST be immediately preceded by a `PUSH`, whose immediate value is the position of its *table*. * The *table* MUST lie within the code, and MUST be named by exactly one *instruction*. * Every *destination* in the *table* of a `JUMPV` MUST be a `JUMPDEST` or a `CALLDEST` *instruction*. Every *destination* in the *table* of a `CALLSUBV` MUST be a `CALLDEST` *instruction*. Immediate data is not an *instruction*. * Each *destination* of a `JUMPV` is a successor of the `JUMPV`, reached at the *stack offset* the `JUMPV` leaves; a `JUMPV` does not fall through. Each *destination* of a `CALLSUBV` is entered as the *destination* of a `CALLSUB` is, and the *instruction* after the `CALLSUBV` is the return point of every one of them. Nothing else changes. In particular, Constraint 4 — one *stack offset* per *instruction* — already requires every *destination* of a `CALLSUBV` to have the same *net stack effect*, since all of them return to one *instruction*; and the sequential scan is the one clients run today, since a *table* is data and not immediate data. ### Costs *high* (10), the tier of `JUMPI`, for both. The work is a bounds comparison, a two-byte read from the code, and the destination check `JUMP` makes; `CALLSUBV` adds the push that `CALLSUB` makes. Benchmarking will be needed to tell if the costs are well-balanced. ## Rationale ### Why is the *table* in the code and its position on the stack? For the reason [EIP-7979](./eip-7979.md) gave for taking no immediate arguments: backwards compatibility.
